method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.

items.assessment: Contralateral cane support is the defensible key; the painful left knee provides side-specific context. Foundation level is appropriate.
Observed walker tipping supports pushing from armrests; competing stabilization, momentum and reach errors have contextual rationales.
Observed pad loading makes axillary compression more likely; handgrip support directly addresses the cue. Fit and symptom reassessment remain sensible follow-up, not competing listed keys.
Locked brakes and feet still on footplates isolate the necessary next preparation; other actions do not establish safe floor contact.
The flaccid limb and movement-related discomfort support avoiding traction through limb support; analgesia does not correct mechanics.
Key is defensible, but stopping all arm movement indefinitely is an implausibly absolute distractor, weakening the choice among range adjustments.
issues: Key is defensible, but stopping all arm movement indefinitely is an implausibly absolute distractor, weakening the choice among range adjustments.
proposedChanges: Replace option 1 with: Repeat the movement after the next analgesic dose without changing the endpoint. Explain that pain relief alone does not make the previously painful range appropriate.

items.assessment: Asymmetric ability supports active practice on the capable side and individualized assistance on the other; passive symmetry is a credible learner error.
Multiple-response key captures timing and alignment; shoulder-first rotation and staffing based solely on body weight are distinct believable errors.
Stable performance at 20 metres and exhaustion at 30 discriminate graded practice from overexertion or complete substitution.
Explicit non-weight-bearing restriction makes even brief loading incorrect; other observations support the plan. Appropriate foundational discrimination.
Sliding pelvis with unsupported feet calls for seating fit review; cushion and exposure-only responses fail to address observed alignment.
Safe bridging and stated functional goal support cueing and participation; staff-only movement would fail to practise retained ability.
Prescribed movement plus neutral positioning targets ankle shortening; knee-only support and reliance on mattress omit the observed problem.
Uses individualized prescribed flexion limit without asserting universal hip precautions; low cushioned chair specifically creates flexion risk.
Fresh painful incision under belt and nonurgent transfer support alternative assessment; padding and analgesia do not resolve mechanical stress.
Seated reachable grooming preserves the client goal and responds to standing-associated breathlessness in stable disease.
Weaker-arm-first key is sound, but finishing faster and waiting for strength to return are weak distractors for a technique question.
issues: Weaker-arm-first key is sound, but finishing faster and waiting for strength to return are weak distractors for a technique question.
proposedChanges: Replace option 0 with: Start with the stronger arm and pull the shirt over the weak elbow. Replace option 2 with: Place the shirt over the head before inserting either arm. Explain how these sequences restrict access or available fabric for the weak limb.

items.assessment: Stronger-arm-first key is sound. Tight sleeves for easier gripping is an implausible adaptive-care recommendation.
issues: Stronger-arm-first key is sound. Tight sleeves for easier gripping is an implausible adaptive-care recommendation.
proposedChanges: Replace option 1 with: Pull the shirt over the head before freeing either arm. Explain that freeing the stronger arm first provides assistance and more fabric movement around the weak limb.

items.assessment: Temporary bending restriction and prescribed reacher make supervised device practice a defensible rehabilitation intervention.
Assessment key is sound but permanently moving all activity to bed is cartoonishly restrictive and easily rejected.
issues: Assessment key is sound but permanently moving all activity to bed is cartoonishly restrictive and easily rejected.
proposedChanges: Replace option 3 with: Continue the same walker and have a helper lift its front legs at the carpet edge. Explain that ad hoc assistance does not first establish route or device suitability.

items.assessment: Schedule and skin inspection are appropriate independent actions; catch-up wear and padding a tight fitted device are credible mistakes.
Tubing slack and unobstructed path directly reduce turn-related traction; emptying containers is an appealing but incomplete safeguard.
Knee rubbing and hip discomfort discriminate limb support from head-only adjustments; context excludes positioning restrictions.
Measured helper requirement matches the stated functional goal more directly than process compliance, range or bed sitting.
Postural symptom/BP assessment is defensible after safe recline. Brand of preadmission footwear is irrelevant filler.
issues: Postural symptom/BP assessment is defensible after safe recline. Brand of preadmission footwear is irrelevant filler.
proposedChanges: Replace option 2 with: The number of ankle exercises completed that morning. Explain that exercise completion does not establish current cardiovascular tolerance of upright positioning.
